questiontext.text: At inference time, what does Byte-Pair Encoding split text into?

feedback.text: Correct — BPE produces subword units between characters and whole words.
No — BPE tokens have variable length driven by learned merges.
No — rare words are broken into smaller subword pieces.
No — BPE operates below the word level, not on sentences.

generalfeedback.text: BPE tokenizes into subword units, balancing vocabulary size against sequence length.

questiontext.text: How does BPE encoding turn a word into tokens?

answer.text: It iteratively merges adjacent symbol pairs using learned merge rules in priority order

feedback.text: Yes — merges are applied greedily following the learned priority.

answer.text: It looks each word up in a fixed dictionary and fails on a miss

feedback.text: No — that cannot handle unknown words; BPE falls back to subwords.

answer.text: It randomly groups characters until a token limit is reached

feedback.text: No — the process is deterministic and rule-driven.

generalfeedback.text: Encoding starts from symbols and repeatedly applies the highest-priority applicable merge rule.

questiontext.text: Why can a trie back a BPE tokenizer?

answer.text: It indexes the vocabulary/merges so shared prefixes are matched efficiently

feedback.text: Correct — a trie shares common prefixes for fast lookup.

answer.text: It sorts the corpus alphabetically before training

feedback.text: No — that is unrelated to a trie's role here.

answer.text: It guarantees every token is exactly one byte

feedback.text: No — tokens are variable-length subwords.

generalfeedback.text: A trie indexes vocabulary entries by shared prefixes, enabling efficient longest-match lookup.

questiontext.text: How does BPE handle a word it never saw during training?

answer.text: It represents the word as a sequence of smaller known subword tokens

feedback.text: Yes — unknown words decompose into known subwords, down to single characters.
No — BPE never drops text; it falls back to subwords.

answer.text: It emits a single fixed UNK token and nothing else

feedback.text: No — subword fallback avoids a lossy single UNK.

generalfeedback.text: Subword fallback lets BPE encode any string, since characters are always in the base vocabulary.

questiontext.text: Which statements about BPE encoding are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It applies learned merge rules in a fixed priority order

feedback.text: Yes — the learned order determines which pair merges first.

answer.text: It balances vocabulary size against sequence length

feedback.text: Yes — larger vocabularies give shorter sequences and vice versa.

answer.text: It requires every input word to appear in the training corpus

feedback.text: No — unknown words are handled via subwords.

answer.text: It merges non-adjacent symbols across the whole word at once

feedback.text: No — merges apply to adjacent pairs, one at a time.

generalfeedback.text: Encoding is ordered, adjacent-pair merging that trades vocabulary size for sequence length and never fails on unknown input.

questiontext.text: During encoding, BPE applies merge rules in a learned priority order rather than arbitrarily.

feedback.text: Correct — the learned priority decides which adjacent pair merges first.
Merges follow the priority order learned during training.

questiontext.text: BPE always emits exactly one token per whole word.

feedback.text: No — words can split into several subword tokens.
Correct — a word may become several subword tokens.

questiontext.text: The core BPE operation that combines an adjacent symbol pair into a new token is called a ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Accepted — the resulting unit is a subword.
Accepted.
